description: Deep study of the microclimate, soil structure, and geological age differences of Burgundy's finest plots

lessons.0.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 1 - 18 minutes
lessons.0.slides.0.description: Understand the components and interactions of terroir from a scientific perspective
lessons.0.slides.1.title: What Is Terroir?
lessons.0.slides.1.content: Terroir is a composite concept encompassing soil, climate, topography, geology, microbial communities, and human factors. In Burgundy, terroir is subdivided to the ultimate degree — different positions within the very same plot can express entirely different characteristics.
lessons.0.slides.2.title: 🔬 The Six Core Elements of Terroir
lessons.0.slides.2.points.0: Geological structure — rock type, stratigraphy, mineral composition
lessons.0.slides.2.points.1: Soil type — texture, depth, drainage, organic matter content
lessons.0.slides.2.points.2: Microclimate — slope aspect, gradient, altitude, wind, sunshine hours
lessons.0.slides.2.points.3: Hydrological conditions — water table, rainfall, soil water-holding capacity
lessons.0.slides.2.points.4: Microbial communities — bacteria, fungi, yeasts in the soil
lessons.0.slides.2.points.5: Human factors — viticultural tradition, winemaking craft, historical heritage
lessons.0.slides.3.title: New World vs. Old World View of Terroir
lessons.0.slides.4.title: Burgundy's Ultimate Expression of Terroir
lessons.0.slides.4.content: Burgundy's Climat system is the ultimate embodiment of terroir philosophy. The 1,247 Climats inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2015 represent a millennium of painstaking observation and delineation. Inside Clos de Vougeot Grand Cru alone, multiple sub-zones are recognised — wines from the upper, middle, and lower slopes differ dramatically in style.
lessons.0.slides.5.title: Historical Evolution of Burgundy's Terroir Classification
lessons.0.slides.6.title: 💡 Key Insights
lessons.0.slides.6.points.0: Terroir is not static — it is a dynamic, evolving ecosystem
lessons.0.slides.6.points.1: The same land in different producers' hands yields different interpretations
lessons.0.slides.6.points.2: Climate change is altering the expression of traditional terroirs
lessons.0.slides.6.points.3: Understanding terroir requires combining scientific knowledge with hands-on tasting
lessons.0.slides.6.points.4: 1,247 Climats represent 1,500 years of accumulated terroir wisdom

lessons.1.title: Influence of Slope Aspect and Altitude
lessons.1.slides.0.title: Influence of Slope Aspect and Altitude
lessons.1.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 2 - 16 minutes
lessons.1.slides.0.description: Understand how topographic factors determine wine quality and style
lessons.1.slides.1.title: Why Does Slope Aspect Matter So Much?
lessons.1.slides.1.content: Nearly all of Burgundy's finest vineyards face east or south-east, at altitudes of 250–350 metres. This orientation delivers the first light of morning while avoiding the harshest afternoon sun, and ensures excellent drainage.
lessons.1.slides.2.title: 🧭 Advantages of Ideal Slope Aspect
lessons.1.slides.2.points.0: East-facing: receives morning sun, gently kickstarts photosynthesis
lessons.1.slides.2.points.1: South-east-facing: extends sunshine hours, increases sugar accumulation
lessons.1.slides.2.points.2: Avoiding west-sun: prevents over-ripening, preserves acidity
lessons.1.slides.2.points.3: Gradient 5–15%: ensures drainage, encourages deep root penetration
lessons.1.slides.2.points.4: Altitude 250–350 m: large diurnal range, full aromatic development
lessons.1.slides.3.title: ⛰️ Côte de Nuits Village Altitude Distribution (the Golden Belt: 250–350 m)
lessons.1.slides.3.content: Most Grand Crus cluster between 280–320 m — the sweet spot for ideal drainage, diurnal range, and sugar/acidity balance.
lessons.1.slides.4.title: Slope Position Differences
lessons.1.slides.5.title: Case Study: The Three Worlds of Clos de Vougeot
lessons.1.slides.5.content: Clos de Vougeot is the finest classroom for understanding slope-position differences. This 50-hectare Grand Cru is shared by more than 80 producers and spans a 60-metre elevation drop from top to bottom. Upper-slope wines (adjacent to Musigny) are elegant and refined; mid-slope wines are balanced; lower-slope wines are fuller and more structured. This explains why the same Clos de Vougeot label can vary in price by 5× or more.
lessons.1.slides.6.title: 📏 Clos de Vougeot: Three-Zone Cross-Section
lessons.1.slides.6.content: 50-hectare Grand Cru divided into upper, middle, and lower zones; altitude drops from 310 m to 250 m. Soil composition, drainage, and wine style differ enormously; prices vary by up to 5×.
lessons.1.slides.7.title: 📍 Famous Upper-Slope Plot Examples
lessons.1.slides.7.points.0: Les Amoureuses (Chambolle-Musigny) — adjacent to Musigny, called 'Grand Cru quality in a Premier Cru'
lessons.1.slides.7.points.1: Les Saint-Georges (Nuits-Saint-Georges) — the village's namesake and finest Premier Cru
lessons.1.slides.7.points.2: Les Perrières (Meursault) — former limestone quarry site; closest white to Grand Cru quality
lessons.1.slides.7.points.3: Clos des Mouches (Beaune) — Joseph Drouhin monopole, excellent in both red and white
lessons.1.slides.7.points.4: Les Caillerets (Volnay) — extreme elegance, very high limestone content
lessons.1.slides.8.title: Effect of Altitude Variation Within the Same Plot

lessons.2.title: The Secrets of Limestone and Marl
lessons.2.slides.0.title: The Secrets of Limestone and Marl
lessons.2.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 3 - 17 minutes
lessons.2.slides.0.description: Understand in depth Burgundy's geological composition and its influence on wine
lessons.2.slides.1.title: Burgundy's Geological Clock
lessons.2.slides.1.content: Burgundy's soils formed principally during the Jurassic period (200–145 million years ago), when the region was a warm, shallow sea. The remains of marine life accumulated into limestone and marl; the precise composition of these rocks determines the style of wine made today.
lessons.2.slides.2.title: 🪨 Three Principal Soil Types
lessons.2.slides.2.points.0: Limestone (Calcaire) — calcium-carbonate rich, superb drainage, imparts minerality
lessons.2.slides.2.points.1: Marl (Marne) — limestone mixed with clay, good water retention
lessons.2.slides.2.points.2: Clay (Argile) — excellent water and nutrient retention, fuller body
lessons.2.slides.2.points.3: Special: Kimmeridgian — unique to Chablis, rich in oyster fossils
lessons.2.slides.2.points.4: White soils (Terres Blanches) — marl-dominant, ideal for white varieties
lessons.2.slides.3.title: 🪨 Typical Grand Cru Soil Composition (Average Ratios)
lessons.2.slides.3.content: Limestone provides minerality and drainage; clay retains water and nutrients; marl (the mixed layer) balances the two. The perfect ratio produces Grand Cru quality.
lessons.2.slides.4.title: Limestone vs. Clay
lessons.2.slides.5.title: The Miracle of Kimmeridgian
lessons.2.slides.5.content: Kimmeridgian soil is the soul of Chablis Grand Cru. Formed in the Late Jurassic (c. 155 million years ago), it is packed with tiny oyster fossils (Exogyra virgula). This unique geology gives Chablis its extreme minerality, saline savour, and shell-like fragrance — a terroir code impossible to replicate elsewhere.
lessons.2.slides.6.title: 💎 Soil Characteristics of Top Plots
lessons.2.slides.6.points.0: Romanée-Conti: red clay with fine gravel, perfect balance of drainage and retention — just 1.81 ha
lessons.2.slides.6.points.1: Le Montrachet: dominantly white limestone, topsoil only 30–40 cm deep, supreme minerality
lessons.2.slides.6.points.2: Clos de Tart: iron-rich red clay, imparts a distinctive spice character
lessons.2.slides.6.points.3: Corton-Charlemagne: white marl — Charlemagne reportedly switched to white to protect his beard from red wine stains
lessons.2.slides.6.points.4: Chablis Grand Cru: Kimmeridgian soil, layer of oyster fossils from 155 million years ago
lessons.2.slides.6.points.5: La Tâche: deep clay, perfect moisture regulation — 6.06 ha monopole
lessons.2.slides.7.title: Burgundy's Geological Ages and Soil Formation
lessons.2.slides.8.title: 🌍 Burgundy's 200-Million-Year Geological Epic
lessons.2.slides.8.content: From warm Jurassic sea to modern vineyard — 200 million years of geological evolution shaped today's terroir. The Kimmeridgian oyster-fossil layer is the very soul of Chablis.
lessons.2.slides.9.title: 🧠 Limestone and Marl Quiz
lessons.3.title: The Precision of Microclimate Control
lessons.3.slides.0.title: The Precision of Microclimate Control
lessons.3.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 4 - 15 minutes
lessons.3.slides.0.description: Understand the microclimate differences between plots within the same village
lessons.3.slides.1.title: Microclimate Determines Quality Difference
lessons.3.slides.1.content: Even within a single village — even in adjacent plots — microclimate differences can cause significant variation in ripeness, acidity, and sugar accumulation. These tiny differences, accumulating over many years, create Burgundy's astonishing terroir diversity.
lessons.3.slides.2.title: 🌡️ Key Factors Influencing Microclimate
lessons.3.slides.2.points.0: Slope angle: a 5-degree change in aspect alters sunshine hours by about 30 minutes
lessons.3.slides.2.points.1: Altitude: temperature falls about 0.6 °C per 100 m rise
lessons.3.slides.2.points.2: Forest windbreak: shields vines from cold winds, moderates temperature
lessons.3.slides.2.points.3: Stone walls (Murs): absorb daytime heat and release it at night
lessons.3.slides.2.points.4: Proximity to water: rivers and lakes regulate temperature, reduce frost risk
lessons.3.slides.3.title: Case Study: The Gentle Secret of Chambolle-Musigny
lessons.3.slides.3.content: Chambolle-Musigny is celebrated as the most elegant village on the Côte de Nuits — the secret lies in its unique microclimate. The village sits in a natural amphitheatre, protected on the east by a forest that shields vines from cold winds. The soil is predominantly limestone: thinner and more impoverished than neighbouring villages, forcing roots to penetrate deep, yielding wines of extraordinary refinement.
lessons.3.slides.4.title: 🍇 Microclimate-Driven Style Differences
lessons.3.slides.4.points.0: Gevrey-Chambertin: open slopes, ample sun, powerful structure
lessons.3.slides.4.points.1: Chambolle-Musigny: sheltered bowl topography, elegance and delicacy
lessons.3.slides.4.points.2: Vosne-Romanée: perfect SE exposure, warm and balanced
lessons.3.slides.4.points.3: Nuits-Saint-Georges: lower altitude, better water retention, stronger structure
lessons.3.slides.4.points.4: Meursault: white soils reflect sunlight, boosting white-grape ripeness
lessons.3.slides.5.title: South-Facing vs. East-Facing Plots
lessons.3.slides.6.title: 🌤️ Measurable Microclimate Differences
lessons.3.slides.6.points.0: Temperature: east vs. south aspect can differ 1–2 °C, shifting ripening by 10–15 days
lessons.3.slides.6.points.1: Sunshine: a 10-degree aspect change alters annual sunshine hours by roughly 100
lessons.3.slides.6.points.2: Wind speed: forest protection reduces wind speed by 30–50%
lessons.3.slides.6.points.3: Frost risk: 100 m altitude difference increases spring frost risk by ~20%
lessons.3.slides.6.points.4: Stone-wall effect: releases stored heat overnight, raising nearby temperatures 0.5–1 °C
lessons.3.slides.7.title: 🧠 Microclimate Precision Quiz
lessons.4.title: Perfect Pairing of Terroir and Grape Variety
lessons.4.slides.0.title: Perfect Pairing of Terroir and Variety
lessons.4.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 5 - 16 minutes
lessons.4.slides.0.description: Understand why Pinot Noir and Chardonnay are the finest interpreters of Burgundy's terroir
lessons.4.slides.1.title: Pinot Noir: Terroir's Transparent Translator
lessons.4.slides.1.content: Pinot Noir is considered the variety most capable of reflecting terroir because it is extraordinarily sensitive to its environment. The very same Pinot Noir clone planted in two plots only 100 metres apart can produce wines that are worlds apart. This hyper-sensitivity is precisely why Burgundy chose Pinot Noir.
lessons.4.slides.2.title: 🍇 Pinot Noir's Terroir Sensitivity
lessons.4.slides.2.points.0: Soil: limestone produces elegance; clay produces power
lessons.4.slides.2.points.1: Aspect: east-facing shows minerality; south-facing shows fruit
lessons.4.slides.2.points.2: Altitude: higher altitude preserves acidity; lower adds body
lessons.4.slides.2.points.3: Vintage: extremely responsive to each year's climate conditions
lessons.4.slides.2.points.4: Winemaking: minimal intervention is the only way to reveal pure terroir
lessons.4.slides.3.title: Pinot Noir vs. Chardonnay Terroir Expression
lessons.4.slides.4.title: Why Does Burgundy Use Only Two Varieties?
lessons.4.slides.4.content: Burgundy's monastic philosophy of simplicity derives from a thousand years of experimentation. Both Pinot Noir and Chardonnay are thin-skinned, early-ripening, and acutely sensitive to terroir. Using a single variety removes the variable of blending, allowing the unique character of each plot to express itself purely. This stands in sharp contrast to the blending philosophy of Bordeaux.
lessons.4.slides.5.title: 💡 Golden Rules of Terroir and Variety
lessons.4.slides.5.points.0: Red: Côte de Nuits Pinot > Côte de Beaune Pinot (structure vs. elegance)
lessons.4.slides.5.points.1: White: Côte de Beaune Chardonnay > Côte de Nuits Chardonnay (complexity vs. freshness)
lessons.4.slides.5.points.2: Exception: Corton-Charlemagne (white) and Corton (red) are both Grand Cru
lessons.4.slides.5.points.3: Chablis: Chardonnay's ultimate expression on Kimmeridgian soil
lessons.4.slides.5.points.4: Beaujolais: Gamay's distinctive character on granite soils
lessons.4.slides.5.points.5: Pinot Noir needs: cool climate + limestone + moderate clay = elegance balanced with power
lessons.4.slides.5.points.6: Chardonnay needs: limestone + excellent drainage = minerality and ageing potential
lessons.4.slides.6.title: Same Variety, Different Terroir — Style Differences
lessons.4.slides.7.title: 🧠 Terroir and Variety Pairing Quiz
lessons.5.title: Climate Change's Impact on Terroir
lessons.5.slides.0.title: Climate Change's Impact on Terroir
lessons.5.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 6 - 18 minutes
lessons.5.slides.0.description: Explore how global warming is transforming Burgundy's traditional terroir expression
lessons.5.slides.1.title: Burgundy Is Warming
lessons.5.slides.1.content: Over the past 30 years, average temperatures in Burgundy have risen by approximately 1.5 °C and the average harvest date has moved forward by two weeks. This has profound implications: plots once considered too cool are now ideal, while traditional top sites face the risk of over-ripening.
lessons.5.slides.2.title: 🌡️ Specific Impacts of Climate Change
lessons.5.slides.2.points.0: Earlier harvest: 1980s average was late September; now early September
lessons.5.slides.2.points.2: Falling acidity: demands more precise timing for harvest decisions
lessons.5.slides.2.points.3: Extreme weather: increased frequency of hail, frost, and heat waves
lessons.5.slides.2.points.4: New pests and diseases: previously unknown threats emerging
lessons.5.slides.3.title: 1990s vs. 2020s
lessons.5.slides.4.title: Producers' Response Strategies
lessons.5.slides.4.content: Facing climate change, Burgundy producers are adapting: selecting higher-altitude or east-facing plots; harvesting earlier to retain acidity; adjusting canopy management to reduce direct sun exposure; experimenting with different clonal selections. Some producers are asking: will the definition of 'ideal terroir' need to be rewritten?
lessons.5.slides.5.title: 🌱 Producers' Adaptation Measures
lessons.5.slides.5.points.0: Vineyard management: more leaf cover to protect grapes from excessive sun
lessons.5.slides.5.points.1: Harvest timing: harvest earlier, sometimes at dawn
lessons.5.slides.5.points.2: Clonal selection: choosing later-ripening clones (e.g. Dijon clones)
lessons.5.slides.5.points.3: Cellar adjustments: lower new-oak percentage, reduce extraction intensity
lessons.5.slides.5.points.4: Long-term strategy: reassessing the potential of marginal plots
lessons.5.slides.6.title: The Future of Terroir
lessons.5.slides.6.content: Climate change is redrawing Burgundy's terroir map. Higher-altitude or north-facing plots once considered secondary may become the new stars. Meanwhile, traditional top sites require ever more meticulous management to maintain quality. This reminds us that terroir is not eternal and unchanging, but a dynamic system that demands continuous understanding and adaptation.
lessons.5.slides.7.title: Timeline of Climate Change Impacts on Burgundy
lessons.5.slides.8.title: 🔮 Future Terroir Trend Predictions
lessons.5.slides.8.points.0: High-altitude plots (350 m+) will become highly prized and rise in price
lessons.5.slides.8.points.1: East- or north-east-facing plots increasingly favoured over traditional south-facing sites
lessons.5.slides.8.points.2: Traditionally 'second-tier' villages (Pernand, Saint-Romain) reassessed for potential
lessons.5.slides.8.points.3: Biodynamic and organic viticulture widespread, strengthening soil climate resilience
lessons.5.slides.8.points.4: Clonal selections shift toward later-ripening, acid-retaining varieties
lessons.5.slides.8.points.5: Harvest pushed back to late August or even mid-August
